cells.note: Systematic-review synthesis of studies conducted in varied surgical educational and performance settings; the study text does not specify participant ages or a common duration.

cells.quote: This review includes studies of a wide range of procedure skill training studies and shows that 15/17 studies have the similar conclusion, that training with an HF simulator does not have outcomes superior to training with an LF simulator.
cells.note: The review reports similar or non-superior outcomes, but does not report an equivalence test or adequate power; therefore direction is coded ns rather than 0.

cells.quote: Review of laparoscopic surgery skill training studies showed that 8/8 concluded that training with an HF simulator did not have outcomes superior to training with LF simulators.
cells.note: This is a subgroup synthesis of eight laparoscopic studies; no equivalence test or adequate power is reported.

cells.quote: These five studies found similar outcomes with LF and HF simulators and that either LF or HF had better outcomes than a control group with no intervention or a group that received didactic training only.
cells.note: The comparison pooled low- and high-fidelity simulation against no intervention or didactic-only control.

O.outcome_detail: skill transfer for junior and senior residents

cells.quote: The authors found that both junior and senior residents had better skill transfer from the bench model to the live animal model after practicing on HF simulators compared to LF simulators.
cells.note: This finding came from one of the 17 reviewed studies and was reported separately by training level.

cells.note: The high-fidelity group was the treatment and performed worse than the low-fidelity comparison on this sub-item.

cells.quote: Both groups improved their theoretical knowledge significantly (p < 0.001), however, no significant intergroup differences were detected (p > 0.05).
cells.note: The study reports no significant between-group difference but does not report an equivalence test or adequate-power basis for coding equivalence.

O.outcome_detail: performance in simulated ventricular-fibrillation ALS scenario

cells.quote: Performance, as assessed by video analysis, was comparable between groups, but, unexpectedly, the low-fidelity group had significantly better results in several sub-items.
cells.note: The low-fidelity group was significantly better on breathing control, continuous chest compression while charging the defibrillator, electrocardiogram analysis, and time interval between electric shocks; most other criteria were comparable.

O.outcome_detail: self-rated confidence and perceived performance relative to actual performance

cells.quote: In this study, participants using HF simulator-training were prone to overrate their abilities and performance, despite showing similar outcomes in theoretical testing and similar, or even inferior, performance of practical skills.
cells.note: The high-fidelity group showed overconfidence: confidence increased without an equivalent increase in knowledge or skill.

O.outcome_detail: belief in learning advantage and fear of being disadvantaged

cells.quote: Before the course (69%) the majority of students in the HF group assumed that they had a significant advantage with regards to their individual learning success, compared to students in the LF group. Participation in the course had no effect on this assumption: 53% of students in the HF group were still convinced of their individual benefit. The difference between pre- and post-course was not statistically significant (p = 0.052). In contrast, we found a significant reduction concerning their fear of being disadvantaged between pre-course (37%) and post-course (13%) (p = 0.003) in the LF group.
cells.note: The reported pre/post findings differ by group: the HF group's perceived advantage did not significantly change, whereas the LF group's fear of disadvantage decreased significantly.

O.outcome_detail: Mean Absolute Deviance (MAD), an observed-versus-predicted fit metric

cells.quote: The fit of the new model, as measured by MAD, is reduced by .012.
cells.note: This is a statistical model comparison based on Geometry Cognitive Tutor log data, not a randomized learning intervention.

D.treatment: LFA model splitting merged Circle into Circle-area and Circle-radius

cells.quote: In BIC model 1, Circle is split into Circle*area, and Circle*radius. The other two BIC models and all the AIC models split it into Circle*backward, and Circle*forward, which are equivalent to Circle-AR*area, and Circle-AR*radius because of the one-to-one relationship between forward and area and between backward and radius. Thus, LFA fully recovers the Circle skills.
cells.note: The contrast is between alternative cognitive-model structures, not learner-assigned instructional conditions.

D.treatment: merged Circle-CD skill for circumference and diameter

cells.quote: None of the models recovered Circle-CD. This suggests that it may not be necessary to have two separate skills for Circle-circumference and Circle-Diameter.
cells.note: The study reports model-selection evidence favoring no recovery of the original distinction, but gives no direct learner-performance effect for this contrast.

D.treatment: splitting Pentagon by initial versus repeated use in a problem
D.comparison: splitting Pentagon by area versus side

cells.quote: In one of the top AIC models, Pentagon is split into Pentagon*initial and Pentagon*repeat, instead of Pentagon*area and Pentagon*side. This suggests that the distinction between the first use of a Pentagon skill in a problem and later uses of that skill in the same problem may be more significant than the distinction between the area and the side.
cells.note: This is a model-selection comparison; the study does not report a learner-level treatment effect.

O.outcome_detail: saving student time while maintaining performance

cells.quote: Much practice spent on an easy skill is not a good use of student time. Reducing the amount of practice for this skill should save student time without compromising their performance.
cells.note: This is a model-based recommendation from observed tutor-log statistics, not a randomized practice-amount intervention.

cells.quote: More practice on this skill is needed for students to reach mastery.

O.outcome_detail: estimated initial, average, and final success probabilities

result.effect: CMarea: initial .64, average .89, final .96; CMsegment: initial .32, average .54, final .60.

cells.note: The contrast is between skills identified by the model split; the study reports observational tutor-log estimates rather than an assigned learner treatment.

D.treatment: LFA-split skill model distinguishing CMarea and CMsegment

O.outcome_detail: estimated success probability for Compose-by-multiplication skills

cells.quote: With final probability .92 students seem to have mastered Compose-by- multimplication. However, the decomposition of the skill shows a different picture. CMarea does well with final probability .96. But CMsegment has final probability only .60 and an average amount of practice less than 2.
cells.note: The study compares alternative cognitive-model representations using tutor log data; it does not report a randomized instructional treatment.

D.treatment: more practice on an under-taught skill

result.effect: Trapezoid-height: initial probability .29, final probability .69, average practice 4.2

cells.quote: Trapezoid-height has a low intercept (-1.55), and a positive slope (.27). Its initial success probability is .29 and the average number of practices per student is 4.2. The final success probability is .69, far away from the level of mastery. More practice on this skill is needed for students to reach mastery.
cells.note: This is a practice recommendation inferred from learning-factor estimates, not an experimentally tested increase in practice.

D.treatment: less practice on an easy skill

cells.quote: Parallelogram-side has a high intercept (2.06) and a low slope (-.01). Its initial success probability is .94 and the average number of practices per student is 14.9. Much practice spent on an easy skill is not a good use of student time. Reducing the amount of practice for this skill should save student time without compromising their performance.
cells.note: The text predicts preserved performance and reduced student time, but reports no intervention testing reduced practice.

D.treatment: improved cognitive model with skill splits

result.effect: Best BIC model: AIC 3888.67, BIC 4248.86, MAD .071; original model: AIC 3950, BIC 4285, MAD .083

cells.quote: All the better models found by AIC and BIC have better (i.e. lower) statistical scores than those of the original. For the best BIC model, its BIC is reduced by 37, and AIC by 62. The fit of the new model, as measured by MAD, is reduced by .012.
